source.title: Scaling Laws For Deep Learning Based Image Reconstruction

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures how image-reconstruction performance scales with training-set size and finds that fitted power-law scaling slows or changes across data-size regimes. It also reports that fitted exponents vary with setup. These results refine the scope of scaling-law claims rather than testing language-model loss scaling directly.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling results, but those cited results are not this study's results and are not rows. It selects the best-performing network size at each training-set size; architecture-size curves used for that selection are not results about V4 or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The paper makes predictions about performance at much larger datasets but does not test those predictions on such runs.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM) against training-set size for U-Net and SwinIR. It does this in denoising, accelerated MRI and super-resolution, scaling network size jointly and picking the best size at each N. It finds a steep power law that bends to a much flatter one at a few thousand images, and explicitly contrasts this with persistent NLP scaling laws. That bears on V5 (image modality) and on V7 (exponents that depend on setup, and curve bending). A linear-estimator analysis adds toy evidence on V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that reconstruction quality follows an initially steep power law in training-set size that slows markedly at moderate sizes (a few thousand images). Interpolation suggests even millions of images would add only marginal in-distribution gains, and architecture improvements (SwinIR over U-Net) exceed expected data-scaling gains. A linear-estimator theory explains this as an error floor once the learning error d/N is small. They note exponents depend on noise and dimensions, and that out-of-distribution results might differ.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales supervised image-reconstruction networks and training sets, measuring PSNR, SSIM, or linear-estimator risk rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. It does not sweep training compute or estimate a parameter/token compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed coefficients and curve shape vary with task, noise level, fixed versus resampled noise, patch size, and (in the theoretical simulations) signal and ambient dimensions.
record.problems: The empirical study covers three image-reconstruction tasks, two architecture families, and in-distribution evaluation; the authors note that results may differ for other architectures, metrics, or out-of-distribution evaluation. For larger training sets, many experiments use one seed. The paper reports error bars over 5 runs for the theoretical simulations, but gives no uncertainty intervals for the empirical fitted coefficients.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Predictions are extrapolated (e.g. 150M or 1.6B images) but never checked against larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation; compute is unlimited and network size is chosen per N.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count; U-Net depth is deliberately not varied.
Video and other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, repeated data; out-of-distribution evaluation.
Downstream task performance vs pretraining loss.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedules and alternative fit methods for LMs.

missing.what: Fixed-noise denoising coefficient α=0.0056 vs 0.0048 for resampled noise
128×128 patch denoising coefficients α=0.005 then 0.0014 (vs 0.0019 for 256×256)
Performance vs network parameters at fixed N is flat or declines for large networks, with no power law in parameters
SwinIR 100k/H benchmark gains of 0.05–0.22 dB over prior SOTA

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 'challenges' label is reversed: bending away from a single power law is what V7 asserts, so those rows support V7. The toy linear/PCA rows are removed from V5, since they are synthetic linear estimators, not another modality's deep models. PSNR is logarithmic in MSE, so the tiny PSNR exponents are not comparable to LM loss exponents. Many large-N runs use a single seed, and the fitted coefficients carry no uncertainty. Some rows mislabel d vs n in Fig. 11 conditions.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
The paper extrapolates to larger image datasets, but does not test predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split is tested.
It scales network sizes, but does not compare depth, width, or architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests supervised image-reconstruction tasks and a synthetic linear denoising model only; it does not test video, other non-image modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not test downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or language-model scale.
Reports sensitivity to task and data/training setup, but does not compare parameter-counting conventions or alternative fitting methods.

relationships.condition: Image denoising (U-Net, SwinIR), MRI and super-resolution in the small-data regime (about 100 to 2.5k–30k images)
relationships.reason: A power law in N fits PSNR/SSIM in the initial regime across tasks and architectures (r1, r3, r5, r7, r9).
relationships.display_finding: Power laws in training-set size fit PSNR and SSIM during the initial regime across reconstruction tasks and architectures.

source_check.reason: Initial power-law fits are explicitly reported for reconstruction quality across these settings. MRI experiments begin at 50 images; PSNR/SSIM coefficients are not language-model loss exponents.

relationships.condition: Same tasks beyond a few thousand images (super-resolution beyond ~30–60k)
relationships.reason: The power law holds under ~2 orders of magnitude, then bends to a 2.5–3x flatter exponent attributed to an error floor (r2, r4, r6, r8, r10).
relationships.display_finding: The initial power law held for fewer than approximately two orders of magnitude before its exponent became 2.5–3× flatter, attributed to an error floor.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Same tasks beyond a few thousand images (super-resolution beyond ~30–60k)
source_check.reason: The initial scaling changes to a flatter regime, warranting qualification. The reason overgeneralizes: σz=15 changes from 0.004 to 0.0026, about 1.54-fold; super-resolution's initial regime spans about 2.5 orders of magnitude from 100 to 30k images.

relationships.condition: Image reconstruction across tasks, noise levels, noise sampling and patch size
relationships.reason: Curves bend from one power law to another (r1/r2, r3/r4, r5/r6, r7/r8). Exponents shift with noise level (r10), fixed noise (r11–r12) and patch size (r14).
relationships.display_finding: Reconstruction curves transition between power laws, while noise level, fixed noise, and patch size change fitted exponents.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Image reconstruction across tasks, noise levels, noise sampling and patch size
source_check.reason: The paired regimes and noise-level comparisons support V7. Figs. 7 and 9 additionally state coefficients for fixed noise and smaller patches; those coefficients should replace reliance on quality-gap rows r11, r12 and r14 alone.

relationships.condition: Synthetic linear subspace denoising (early-stopped GD and PCA estimators)
relationships.reason: Exponents change with noise, n and d. Fitting R vs R−R* changes the exponent, e.g. −2.4 vs −1.0 at σz=0.05 (r15–r38).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents vary with noise, n, and d, and fitting R versus R−R* changes the exponent from −2.4 to −1.0 at σz=0.05.
